main.text: [II, 787] [col. 197] Chapter X.
The names of the raven, its voice, colour, abode, food, kinds, etc.

The raven, which we must now treat, has two features that most force themselves upon the senses: [col. 198] its croaking and its blackness. Croaking, in Greek κρωγμὸς [krōgmos], is a hoarse and harsh sound drawn from the depths of the throat, which ravens repeat over and over with great effort, as if in competition; above all when they foretell rains and storms. Hence Nicander, Theriaca, line 406:
Αἰγυπιοὶ, γῦπές τε, κόραξ τ᾽ ὀμβρήρεα κρώζων, [Aigypioi, gypes te, korax t᾽ ombrērea krōzōn,]
Aegypii, and vultures, and the raven croaking of rain, that is, announcing rainy weather to come by its croaking. Lucretius, book 5, line 1082:

And in part they change together with the weather The hoarse-sounding songs of the crows, and the long-lived generations, And the flocks of ravens, when they are said to call for Waters and rains, and at times to summon winds and breezes.

Blackness, too, is proper to the raven, and that most intense, and spread over its whole body. Yet what Porphyry writes in chapter 5 of the Isagoge is not true without exception: Τὸ δὲ μέλαν εἶναι ἀχωρίστως τῷ κόρακι καὶ τῷ Αἰθίοπι συμβέβηκε· [To de melan einai achōristōs tō koraki kai tō Aithiopi symbebēke;] Blackness is so present in the raven and the Ethiopian that it cannot be separated. For white ravens too have been seen. Aristotle, On the Generation of Animals, book 5, chapter 6: Ὦπται καὶ πέρδιξ λευκὴ, καὶ κόραξ· [Ōptai kai perdix leukē, kai korax;] A white partridge has been seen, and a raven. Heraclides in the Constitution of Cyrene: Ἀρκεσιλάου δὲ βασιλεύοντος λευκὸς κόραξ ἐφάνη· [Arkesilaou de basileuontos leukos korax ephanē;] When Arcesilaus was king, a white raven appeared. Such are found even today in Sweden and Norway, where the cold is more intense. Yet it is admitted that a white raven is rarely found. Hence Juvenal, Satire 7:
Yet he is fortunate, rarer even than a white raven.
And Ammianus in the Anthology, book 2, chapter 46, Epigram 17:
Θᾶττον ἔην λευκοὺς κόρακας, πτηνάς τε χελώνας Εὑρεῖν, ἢ δόκιμον ῥήτορα Καππαδόκην· [Thatton eēn leukous korakas, ptēnas te chelōnas heurein, ē dokimon rhētora Kappadokēn;]

It is easier to find white ravens and flying tortoises than a good orator from Cappadocia. Therefore, as these two things, croaking, I say, and blackness, are most proper to the raven, so most of the raven's names are taken from one or the other. Thus from croaking comes ܢܥܒܐ neab; and in Arabic نعاب [nuʿāb] noab, namely from the verb نعب [naʿaba] naaba, which means to croak. And in the Ethiopic name of the raven, ቋዕ፡ [II, 788] koe, there is a manifest imitation of the raven's voice. From the same source arose the Greek κόραξ [korax], as well as κρώζειν [krōzein]; and the Roman crocire and crocitare. For those are mistaken who would have κόραξ [korax] so called παρὰ τὸν κόρον, ὃ σημαίνει τὸ μέλαν [para ton koron, ho sēmainei to melan], since κόρος [koros] in the sense of black occurs nowhere among the ancients. But the Hebrew עורב oreb, the Chaldee ערבא orba, and the Arabic غراب [ghurāb] gorab (whence the Romans said corvus) plainly relate to colour. For in Hebrew ערב ereb is evening, and ערב arab, the verb, is to grow towards evening, to grow dark. Hence in Arabic غربيب [ghirbīb] garbib is black (the initial Ain being changed into Gain by the added dot); so here the same thing happens as with the Greek words δνοφερὸς [dnopheros], ὄρφνιος [orphnios] and ὄρφνινος [orphninos], which are transferred from darkness to signify [col. 199] blackness. And from the dark, or, what is the same, black colour, the Hebrews called the raven עורב oreb, and the Arabs غراب [ghurāb] gorab. Meanwhile it must be acknowledged that the κοράκινον [korakinon], or raven-coloured, has some lustre, whereas the dusky colour is ἄστιλπνος [astilpnos]. That is why Vitruvius, book 8, chapter 3, distinguishes raven-black from dusky in these words: Though they are white, in some places they produce grey-white, in other places dusky, in others raven-black. And learned men define κοράκινον χρῶμα [korakinon chrōma] as a deepest black with some sheen, such as that of jet and of our velvet. Strabo, book 12, attributes this colour to the wool around Laodicea in Phrygia, saying that region bears προβάτων ἀρετὰς, οὐκ εἰς μαλακότητας μόνον τῶν ἐρίων, ᾗ καὶ τῶν Μιλησίων διαφέρει, ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰς τὴν κόραξιν χρόαν [probatōn aretas, ouk eis malakotētas monon tōn eriōn, hē kai tōn Milēsiōn diapherei, alla kai eis tēn koraxin chroan], excellent sheep, not only in the softness of their wool, in which they surpass even the Milesian, but also in colour, such as is in ravens. For one must read τὴν ἐν κόραξιν χρόαν [tēn en koraxin chroan]; but after τὴν [tēn] that ἐν [en] was omitted, because τὴν [tēn] and ἐν [en] are nearly ὁμοιόπτωτοι [homoioptōtoi]. This colour is also pleasing in hair. Hence in Apuleius, book 2, hair is praised as dark-blue with raven blackness: coerulus, that is, black, as in Greek κυάνεος [kyaneos]. So even one who has hair made black by art is compared with the raven. Martial, book 3, Epigram 43:
You feign youth with dyed hair, Lentinus, so suddenly a raven, you who were lately a swan.
And Alcibiades, lisping, says of Theorus in Aristophanes, in the Wasps:
Ὁλᾷς Θέωλον τὴν κεφαλὴν κόλακος ἔχει, [Holas Theōlon tēn kephalēn kolakos echei,]

κόλακος [kolakos], that is, of a flatterer, attributing to him the head of a flatterer instead of κόρακος [korakos], that is, of a raven; because he could not pronounce R otherwise than as L. But there follows,
Ὀρθῶς γε τοῦτ᾽ Ἀλκιβιάδης ἐθραύλισεν [Orthōs ge tout᾽ Alkibiadēs ethraulisen],

This Alcibiades lisped rightly; because in truth Theorus was a notorious flatterer. All this serves to show why it is said of the bridegroom in Cant. V, 2: קוצותיו תלתלים שחורות כעורב, His locks are hanging, black as a raven. For so we interpret it: [II, 789] because in Arabic قُصَّة [quṣṣa] Kutssa is the portion of the hair that overhangs the forehead, or hangs down from the front part of the head. And we explain תלתלים, with Solomon, as hanging, as if a reduplicated form of the verb תלה, which means to hang. Thus from יפה reduplicated comes יפיפית, thou art fair, Ps. XLV, 3. Those locks, then, which hang down over the forehead, ears and cheeks, are said to be black as a raven, that is, of raven colour, which is conspicuous for its sheen. Nor is it obscure why he mentions only the locks. The subject is a crowned king: accordingly it is said in Cant. III, 11. Behold, daughters of Zion, King Solomon with the crown with which his mother crowned him on the day of his espousals. And in this very verse: His head of finest gold (supply crowned), his locks hanging, black as a raven. This is almost the only part of the hair that is visible when the head is encircled with a crown. Moreover, everyone knows that it belongs to beauty of appearance that the hair should shine with a raven colour; hence some strive after it with the greatest zeal, and the curious seek remedies from the raven itself by which to obtain it. Hence Pliny, book 29, chapter 6: A raven's egg, mixed in a bronze vessel and smeared on the shaven head, gives blackness to the hair, etc. And a little later: Others use its blood and brain with dark wine. Others boil the bird itself down and at dead of night store it in a lead vessel. And Aelian, Hist. book 1, chapter 48: Προσακούω δὲ καὶ ὠὰ κόρακος μελαίνειν τρίχας [Prosakouō de kai ōa korakos melainein trichas]; I hear that raven's eggs make the hair black. The same things are prescribed by Sextus, Marcellus, Rhazes, and not a few other Arabs. Rightly, therefore, Solomon's appearance is praised in the Song for his having black hair, indeed black like a raven, that is, of raven colour. If you object that in [col. 200] this book Solomon is set before us as a type of Christ, who on the contrary in Dan. VII, 9. and Apoc. I, 14. is described as old and with white hair, I reply that both befit Christ in different respects. For as black hair signifies youthful vigour, so white hair signifies the gravity and wisdom of age. The Arabs call the blackness of the raven حلك [ḥalak] chalac, or حنك [ḥanak] chanac, a most proper term. Alcamus: حلك الغراب حنكه او سواده [ḥalak al-ghurāb ḥanakuhu aw sawāduhu], Chalac of the raven, that is, chanac, or its blackness. And elsewhere: حنك الغراب منقاره او سواده [ḥanak al-ghurāb minqāruhu aw sawāduhu], Chanac of the raven: its beak, or its blackness. Likewise, اسود حانك حالك [aswad ḥānik ḥālik], Black, chanic, chalic, that is, very black, like the raven, whose blackness is most intense.

That the raven is an animal fond of solitude is generally agreed. Accordingly Hesychius has: Σκορακίζει· εἰς ἔρημον πέμπει, καὶ ἀρᾶται, ἀπὸ τοῦ εἰς κόρακας πέμπειν [Skorakizei; eis erēmon pempei, kai aratai, apo tou eis korakas pempein]. The sense is that to send to the ravens is the same as to curse someone, wishing that he be banished and relegated to the wilderness. Of the same kind is the remark of the Scholiast on Aristophanes in the Clouds, on the proverb Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρ κας [Ball᾽ es kor kas], that ravens ἐν τοῖς ἐρημοτέροις τόποις ἐπιτηρεῖν τὰ σώματα [en tois erēmoterois topois epitērein ta sōmata], watch for corpses in solitary places. Here too [II, 790] belongs the prediction in Es. XXXIV, 10, that after Idumaea has been laid waste, the owl and the raven will dwell in the ruins of its metropolis Bosra. To this is added Sophon. II, 14, on the devastation of Nineveh: The voice of one singing in the window, the raven on the lintel. For so Jerome has it. And the version of the Greeks: Θηρία φωνήσει ἐν τοῖς διορύγμασιν αὐτῶν, καὶ κόρακες ἐν τοῖς πυλῶσιν αὐτῆς [Thēria phōnēsei en tois diorygmasin autōn, kai korakes en tois pylōsin autēs]; Beasts will cry out in their (the Ninevites') ditches, and ravens in her gates (Nineveh's). And Theodoret, on this passage, counts among the signs of devastation κοράκων νεοττίαι [korakōn neottiai], nests of ravens. And Cyril understands by the ravens night-ravens, which would not dwell in the very gates of the city unless there were a great deal of quiet and leisure there, which is most agreeable to their nature: Οὐδ᾽ ἂν ἐμφιλοχωρήσειαν αὐτοῖς πυλῶσιν οἱ νυκτικόρακες, εἰ μὴ πλείστη τις ὅση καὶ ἁνδάνουσα λίαν τοῖς ὧδε φύσεως ἔχουσιν ὑπάρχῃ σχολή [Oud᾽ an emphilochōrēseian autois pylōsin hoi nyktikorakes, ei mē pleistē tis hosē kai handanousa lian tois hōde physeōs echousin hyparchē scholē]. But the Hebrew word חרב choreb, which they explain as raven ^{(1)}, means dryness and devastation; or, if you read chereb, sword. Accordingly the Syriac translator renders it sword, as does Aquila too. And others among the Greeks render it dryness, as Jerome attests; why he preferred to render it raven, I cannot grasp at all. In the Hebrew (he says) is written חרב, which, according to the difference of reading, is taken as either dryness, or sword, or raven. As if חרב with Cheth and ערב with Ajin were the same. No one would grant Jerome that. For ערב, with Ajin and Cholem, means raven; but חרב, with Cheth and Cholem, means dryness and devastation, or sword if it has Segol. Since here, then, they write חרב with Cheth and Cholem, the words of Zephaniah are to be rendered thus: A voice will resound from the window; devastation will be on the threshold, when the cedar has been laid bare, that is, the cedar panelling. By voice here I understand one such as in Es. XIII, 21.

Here it may be asked why Solomon calls ravens ערבי נחל, ravens of the valley, or, if you prefer, ravens of the torrent, Prov. XXX, 17. For נחל means both valley and torrent ^{(2)}. I would take it as ravens of the valley, with the Greeks, who have κόρακες ἐκ τῶν φαράγγων [korakes ek tōn pharangōn], that is, ravens from the valleys, or those that like to nest in secluded valleys, which in Hebrew you might rightly call נחלי הבתות, valleys of the wastes [II, 791], with the Prophet Es. VII, 19. One may also understand some particular valley frequented by ravens and named after them. Isaiah could be understood of some such valley, were it not for the Masoretes, when he says of the riches of the Moabites, Es. XV, 7: על נחל הערבים ישאום, that is, as it is commonly rendered, They will carry them to the valley of the Arabs, or to the torrent of willows. And that indeed rightly, since the vowels supplied by the Masoretes [col. 201] do not allow us to interpret otherwise. But if they were absent, one could just as well read, They will carry them to the valley of the ravens. In this sense it is said in Greek Βάλλ᾽ ἐς κόρακας [Ball᾽ es korakas], that is, εἰς ἀπώλειαν, καὶ εἰς φθοράν [eis apōleian, kai eis phthoran]. And in Isaiah himself, II, 20, to cast idols to the moles and the bats is to destroy and cut them off. Now, if one may indulge in conjecture, that valley of the ravens was the very one that is called the valley of corpses in Ierem. XXXI, 40. And the same valley was called by both names because ravens, flocking together from every side, consumed the corpses of the condemned thrown into it. Granting this, when Solomon says that the ravens of the valley will pick out the eye that mocks its father, it will be as if he had said that one guilty of so foul a crime, having suffered an infamous punishment, is to be thrown into the valley of corpses, to be consumed there by ravens. For it counts as part of the penalty for the guilty that their corpses lie unburied or hang, to be torn apart by wild beasts or by carnivorous birds. Hence in Aristophanes' Θεσμοφορούσαις [Thesmophorousais] Mnesilochus begs to be spared punishment on this account, that he, an old man, should not be laughed at by the women τοῖς κόραξιν ἑστιῶν [tois koraxin hestiōn], providing a banquet for ravens. And shortly after, Ἐκρέμασε κόραξι δεῖπνον [Ekremase koraxi deipnon], He hung him up, to be a dinner for ravens. Horace too, Epistle 16 to Quintius,
— — — you will not feed the ravens on the cross:
as in Philostratus' Heroica, and Tzetzes, Chil. 5, ch. 22, the Centaur Asbolus,
Ὑψικόμοιο κρεμαστὸς ἀπ᾽ εὐλιπέος κατὰ πεύκης Σύγκειται, μέγα δεῖπνον ἀμετροβίοις κοράκεσσιν· [Hypsikomoio kremastos ap' eulipeos kata peukēs synkeitai, mega deipnon ametrobiois korakessin]
He hangs fixed to the trunk of a lofty pine, to give a sweet banquet to the insatiable ravens.

And Solomon mentions the eye by name: The eye, he says, that mocks its father, the ravens of the valley shall dig out; for the raven goes for the eye above all. And, as Isidore attests, first (read primo) it goes for the eye in corpses. Hence Epictetus: Οἱ μὲν κόρακες τῶν τετελευτηκότων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς λυμαίνονται· [Hoi men korakes tōn teteleutēkotōn tous ophthalmous lymainontai] Ravens ravage the eyes of the dead. (See the rest in the chapter On the eagle ^{a)}.) Catullus too, calling down death on Cominius, adds this:

Let the raven devour his dug-out eyes with its black gullet, the dogs his entrails, the wolves his other limbs. [II, 792] What of the fact that they do not spare even the eyes of the living? Hence Aristophanes in the Birds:
Ὁ κόραξ παρελθὼν τοῦπιορκοῦντος λάθρα Προσπτάμενος ἐκκόψει τὸν ὀφθαλμὸν θένων· [Ho korax parelthōn toupiorkountos lathra prosptamenos ekkopsei ton ophthalmon thenōn]
Let the raven, coming up and flying at him unseen, strike and dig out the eye of the perjurer. Likewise:

Οἱ δ' αὖ κόρακες τῶν ζευγαρίων, οἷσι τὴν γῆν καταροῦσι, Καὶ τῶν προβάτων τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς ἐκκοψάντων· [Hoi d' au korakes tōn zeugariōn, hoisi tēn gēn katarousi, kai tōn probatōn tous ophthalmous ekkopsantōn]

Again, let the ravens pluck out the eyes of the yoked oxen with which they plough the land, and of the sheep. And Gregory of Nyssa, Homily 13, calls the raven σαρκοβόρον τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν ἀφανιστικὸν [sarkoboron tōn ophthalmōn aphanistikon], a flesh-eater, a destroyer of eyes. And Alkazuinius, in the chapter غراب [ghurāb] gorab, or On the Raven: يجتمع علي كل الحيوانات الكبار البادية كالجمل والفرس وكذا الادمي ويقصد قلع عينها ولا يمتنع بالدفع والضرب لشدة جوعه [yajtamiʿ ʿalī kull al-ḥayawānāt al-kibār al-bādiya ka-l-jamal wa-l-faras wa-kadhā al-ādamī wa-yaqṣid qalʿ ʿaynihā wa-lā yamtaniʿ bi-l-dafʿ wa-l-ḍarb li-shiddat jūʿihi] It settles on all the large animals that are in the open country, such as camels and horses, and even on men, and tries to pluck out their eyes; nor is it kept off by driving away or beating, because of the violence of its hunger. Although this is not peculiar to the raven, if Cardanus writes truly in book 7, chapter 35 of De rerum varietate: No kind of large bird, whether hens, or peacocks, or ravens, or cranes, or [col. 202] storks, becomes so tame that, if they are rather close, they do not try to tear out your eyes. I have heard the same about ostriches from those who lead them about. And Pliny gives this reason, book 11, ch. 37: And so perfect is the mirror-like power in the eyes that that tiny pupil gives back the whole image of a man. This is the reason why most birds, when in men's hands, go chiefly for the eyes: seeing their own likeness in them, they make for them as if toward the objects of their natural longing. Meanwhile an old proverb is bandied about, A raven does not pluck out a raven's eye. Gregory of Tours on King Chilperic (History, book 5, ch. 18): And on seeing me the king said, "O bishop, you ought to bestow justice on all; and, behold! I do not receive justice from you. But, as I see, you consent to iniquity, and in you is fulfilled that proverb, 'A raven does not pluck out a raven's eye.'" By this proverb he was hinting that Bishop Gregory had been unwilling to pronounce anything against another bishop accused of high treason.

From what has been said it is plainly evident that τὸ σκορακίζειν [to skorakizein], or to send or cast to the ravens, is not only what Hesychius defined above, to wish on someone withdrawal or banishment into the wilderness, but also to devote him to death and to wish him every extremity. Yet among the sacred writers σκορακίζειν [skorakizein] and ἀποσκορακίζειν [aposkorakizein] mean only to abandon, to repel, to rebuke. And σκορακισμὸς [skorakismos], or ἀποσκορακισμὸς [aposkorakismos], means repulse and rebuke. Thus Eccles. XLI, 19. (Αἰσχύνεθε [Aischynethe]) ἀπὸ σκορακισμοῦ λήψεως, καὶ δόσεως· [apo skorakismou lēpseōs, kai doseōs] Be ashamed on account of the rejection of what is given [II, 793] and received. The Septuagint, Psal. XXVI, 9. Μὴ ἀποσκορακίσῃς με ^{(3)}· [Mē aposkorakisēs me] Do not forsake me: Hebrew אל תטשני. Esa. XVII, 13. Καὶ ἀποσκορακιεῖ αὐτόν· [Kai aposkorakiei auton] Hebrew וגער בו, And he rebuked him. Es. LXVI, 15. Καὶ ἀποσκορακισμὸν ἐν φλογὶ πυρός· [Kai aposkorakismon en phlogi pyros] in Hebrew וגערתו בלהבי אש, And his rebuke in a flame of fire. But there rebuke is taken for destruction, as often among the Hebrews. Yet Cyril explains it as ἀποβολὴν [apobolēn], rejection, because God will say to the reprobate, Depart from me, you cursed, into the eternal fire.

Moses forbids the raven to the Jews למינו, after its kind, or after its species, as he does certain other birds in the list of the unclean. And, as R. Selomo notes, when after its kind is added to the name of a bird, יש באותו המין שאין דומין זה לזה לא כמראיהם ולא בשמותיהם וכולן מין אחד, it has species unlike in form and name, which are nevertheless referred to one kind. But we shall show below that this is hardly well founded. Still, if you ask for the species of ravens, there may be referred to it the crow, the graculus [jackdaw], the jackdaw, the magpie, and even the starling, if one believes Baal Hatturim, who relies on a Cabbalistic argument: namely, that the words עורב למינו, the raven after its kind, and the word זרזר, that is, starling, are ἰσόψηφα [isopsēpha]. For both amount to 414. The Arabs in Damir describe the species of the raven thus: والغربان اربعة اجناس اسود حالك وابلق ومطرف ببياض لطيف الجرم ياكل الحب واسود طاووسي براق الريش ورجلاه بلون المرجان يعرف بالزاغ [wa-l-ghirbān arbaʿat ajnās aswad ḥālik wa-ablaq wa-muṭarraf bi-bayāḍ laṭīf al-jirm yaʾkul al-ḥabb wa-aswad ṭāwūsī barrāq al-rīsh wa-rijlāhu bi-lawn al-marjān yuʿraf bi-l-zāgh], There are four species of ravens. 1. The perfectly black (this is the raven properly so called). 2. The pied, or mixed of black and white (I understand the crow which in our vernacular we call the palliata [hooded]). 3. The one that has white extremities, slender in body, feeding on grains (that is, the σπερμολόγος [spermologos] crow). 4. The peacock-like black one, with shining plumage and coral-coloured feet, which is called the magpie. That the Arabs [col. 203] refer the crow to the raven kind is clearest from the fact that they consistently call the plant κορωνόπους [korōnopous] رجل الغراب [rijl al-ghurāb] raven's foot.

One of the princes of Midian was called עורב Oreb, that is, raven. And the place in which he was slain by the Ephraimites is the Rock of Oreb, Iudic. VII, 25. and Esa. X, 26. Likewise Κόρακος πέτρη [Korakos petrē], the rock of Corax, or of the raven, was a place on Ithaca, at which ὁ Κόραξ κυνηγῶν ἀπὸ τῆς πέτρας πεσῶν ἐτελεύτησε [ho Korax kynēgōn apo tēs petras pesōn eteleutēse], a certain hunter Corax (that is, named raven) died after falling from the rock. So the old Scholiast on the verse of Homer, Odyss. 13:
Παρ' Κόρακος πέτρῃ, ἐπί τε κρήνῃ Ἀρεθούσῃ. [Par' Korakos petrē, epi te krēnē Arethousē.]

notes.text: This very thing is denied by I. E. Faber in his dissertation On the animals mentioned in Zephan. II, 14., at the end of Cramer's book entitled Scythische Denkmaehler in Palaestina, p. 304. He maintains that the name κορακος [korakos] was put by the translators for קאת, and that of χαμαιλεωντος [chamaileōntos] for חרב: both without adequate reason, and for no other purpose than to defend his own flimsy conjectures about the names of those animals. Compare above p. 507, note, and 509, note.

נחל is a low-lying place in the deserts, like a riverbed, through which a torrent rushes in the rainy season, but which is dry for the rest of the year, Arab. وادي [wādī]; the Arabic translator in the Polyglots rightly uses this very word for the Hebr. נחל at Num. XIII, 23. See on these valleys Niebuhr, Descript. Arab. p. 2; Della Valle, Travels vol. 4, p. 183 b, German trans.; Oedmann, Vermischte Sammlungen, vol. 5, Chapter 13, pp. 116–117.

So it is written in the Aldine and Complutensian text, in place of what is commonly read in our editions, simply: μη ἐγκαταλιπῃς με [mē enkatalipēs me]. See Lamb. Bos on the passage. Biel has gathered a good deal on the etymology of the verb ἀποσκορακίζειν [aposkorakizein] in his Thesaurus, under that word.
